headline: Amanpour leaves CNN after 43 years. No reason given.
summary: Christiane Amanpour, CNN's chief international anchor, said Monday she will leave the network in June 2027. Her nightly CNN International show goes weekly in January and ends in May. Her PBS show ends this year. She gave no reason. The exit comes two weeks after Skydance closed its $81 billion buyout of CNN's parent. She joined in 1983.

cover_question.q: Why is she leaving her job?

cover_answer: She didn't say. After 43 years, she wants new projects.
table_question: When is the right time to stop doing something you're good at?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: A woman called Christiane Amanpour has told people the news on TV for 43 years, since before most of your teachers were born. She flew to places where wars were happening and told everyone far away what she saw. Now she has decided to stop next year and try new things. She is fine. She picked her own time to go.
5-7.why: The job, told as flying off to look and telling everyone. A six-year-old needs the person to be fine, so the script says so.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old takes one vivid feature for the whole, so the script gives them the job as a picture: flying to where the trouble is and telling everyone far away. Leaving a job can sound like being sent away, so the script says she chose, and that she is fine. Expect "did she get in trouble?" No. She decided. Her boss said thank you.

8-12.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
8-12.script: In 1983 one of Amanpour's bosses told her she didn't have what it took to be a foreign correspondent. She became CNN's best-known war reporter anyway, from the Gulf War to Ukraine. At 68, she has set her own leaving date. One wrong call against a scoreboard 43 years long.
8-12.why: A wrong boss and a long scoreboard. Kids this age keep score.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out whether adults judge fairly, so the script runs the chain they can check: one boss said no, the record said otherwise for 43 years. The scoreboard is the mechanism, evidence outlasting an opinion. Expect "why leave if she's so good?" She didn't say. Her boss says they talked for months and it is the right time.

13-17.script: Amanpour's rule is "always be truthful, not neutral." Can a reporter be both, or does one give? Second: she gave no reason for leaving, and the news came two weeks after an $81 billion merger gave CNN a new owner. Coincidence, or the reason she didn't say?
13-17.why: Her own rule, then the timing. Follow the evidence with them.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: Amanpour gave no reason, and the timing sits two weeks after the merger. The script asks them to argue from that without inventing the rest, the skill Kuhn says gets practised, not taught. Expect "so was she pushed?" Nobody has said so. Say that plainly and leave the gap open.

5-7.q: Why is she leaving her job?
5-7.a: She didn't say why. After 43 years she wants to try new projects. Her boss said thank you and that everyone will be sad to see her go.

8-12.q: What does a chief international anchor do?
8-12.a: Reports the news from other countries, on her own show.
Not quite. She wants new projects, and keeps her podcast.

13-17.q: Did the merger push her out?
13-17.a: Nobody has said so. She gave no reason. The timing is all anyone has.
Report what the evidence shows, even when it favours one side. Is that taking sides?
